Just before noon on Thursday, the USS Abraham Lincoln slid up to the pier at Naval Air Station North Island in San Diego, water cannons arcing over her flight deck and helicopters circling overhead. Hundreds of families crowded the waterfront, shouting and waving, many of them meeting sailors and Marines they had not seen in the better part of a year.

They had waited a long time. The Lincoln pulled out of San Diego last November for what was supposed to be a routine Pacific cruise. It became anything but. 

Redirected to the Middle East and handed two separate extensions, the carrier ended up away from home for 322 days, close to 11 months, with more than 200 of those days spent in a combat zone. At one stretch she went 286 straight days without a single port call, which the Navy considers a modern-day record.

What the crew did out there earned the strike group the Presidential Unit Citation, pinned on the day before they pulled in. But the number that mattered most on the pier was simpler. “Every sailor and Marine who deployed is returning,” said the carrier’s commanding officer, Capt. Daniel Keeler, who called the crew’s performance legendary. The ship came home with no lives lost, no aircraft lost, and no combat damage.

For the families, it was enough that the ship was finally tied up and the ramp was coming down. “They are all heroes,” said Carla Smith, whose son serves aboard the Lincoln, as she waited for him to step ashore.

The first two of Taiwan's new F-16V fighter jets touched down on October 2, 2026, at Chihhang Air Base in Taitung, the opening delivery of a 66-aircraft order built by Lockheed Martin. Flown across the Pacific with stops in Hawaii and Guam, the jets are the newest Block 70 version of the F-16, fitted with advanced radar, avionics, and weapons designed to counter China's air force, including its stealthy J-20 fighters.

The 66 jets were approved in 2019 under an $8 billion deal, though software issues pushed back the first deliveries. Once the full order is complete, Taiwan's F-16 fleet will grow to more than 200 aircraft. "This is an important development in strengthening Taiwan's air defense," said President Lai Ching-te.

Roosevelt Heads Out

The aircraft carrier USS Theodore Roosevelt departed San Diego this week, starting a deployment expected to run more than 7 months. The ship is bound for the Middle East, where it will take over duty from the USS George Washington and keep a carrier on station in the region.

A Nimitz-class, nuclear-powered carrier, the Roosevelt sends thousands of sailors and a full air wing to sea for the length of the cruise. Once the handoff is complete, the George Washington is set to head home.

Their tanks were made of rubber and could be lifted by two men. Their artillery couldn't fire a shot. Their "army" was largely an illusion. And yet this secret unit of American artists, designers, and sound engineers pulled off one of the most ingenious operations of World War II, tricking the German army again and again, and saving thousands of lives in the process. For 40 years, almost no one knew they existed. This is the story of the "Ghost Army."

AN ARMY OF ARTISTS

Officially, they were the 23rd Headquarters Special Troops. Unofficially, they became known as the Ghost Army, and they were unlike any military unit before them.

Activated in early 1944, the roughly 1,100-man unit was deliberately filled not with typical combat soldiers, but with creative minds: painters, illustrators, designers, engineers, sound technicians, and theater people, recruited from art schools, advertising agencies, and the entertainment industry. Among its members were men who would go on to be famous, including the celebrated fashion designer Bill Blass and renowned artists. It was, in a sense, an army of imagination.

Their mission was as unusual as their makeup: to deceive the enemy. Specifically, to impersonate other, much larger American units, to make the Germans believe powerful forces were somewhere they weren't, and to hide where the real forces actually were. A unit of 1,100 men learned to convincingly fake the presence of two entire divisions, some 30,000 troops.

THE FOUR TRICKS OF THE TRADE

The Ghost Army worked its magic using four kinds of illusion, woven together like instruments in an orchestra of deception.

First was the visual. The unit built and deployed hundreds of inflatable tanks, trucks, jeeps, cannons, and even aircraft, rubber decoys that, from a distance or from the air, looked exactly like a massive armored force. The props were so light that a couple of soldiers could pick up a "tank" and carry it, and they had to be tied down so a strong wind wouldn't send the army tumbling across the field.

Second was sound. A specialized unit mounted enormous speakers on trucks and blasted prerecorded audio, the rumble of tank columns, the clatter of construction, the voices of troops, across the countryside. The sounds could be heard for miles, convincing the enemy that a huge force was moving or massing nearby, when in reality there was almost nothing there.

Third was radio. Skilled operators sent out fake radio transmissions, mimicking the Morse-code chatter of real units, knowing the Germans were listening in. By faking the communications of a division, they could make that division seem to appear out of thin air.

And fourth was pure theater. The men would actually pose as soldiers from the units they were impersonating, sewing on the right patches, painting the correct markings on their vehicles, and even lounging in local cafes loudly telling cover stories, in case enemy spies were listening. They became method actors in a life-or-death performance.

DANGEROUS WORK

It's tempting to think of this as a lighthearted assignment, but it was anything but. The Ghost Army operated close to the front lines, sometimes within earshot of the enemy, and they did it with almost no real weapons to defend themselves. Their entire protection was the illusion. If the Germans had ever seen through the trick and attacked, these artists and sound men, armed with rubber tanks, would have been nearly helpless.

They knew it, too. If the enemy discovered they were being made fools of, the retaliation could have been brutal. Every deception was a gamble with their lives.

DID IT WORK?

Spectacularly. Over the final year of the war, the Ghost Army staged more than 20 elaborate deceptions across France, Belgium, Luxembourg, Germany, and Italy. Time and again, they drew enemy attention toward forces that didn't exist, or masked the movements of the real ones.

Their masterpiece came in March 1945, when they faked a major river crossing of the Rhine, drawing German defenders toward the Ghost Army's illusion and away from the point where real American troops would actually cross. Their trickery worked so well that, remarkably, the enemy never once figured out the deception during the entire war.

Historians estimate that the illusions of this tiny unit saved somewhere between 15,000 and 30,000 American lives, soldiers who were spared because the enemy was looking the wrong way, or bracing for an attack that was never coming, or defending against a force made of rubber and sound.

SECRET FOR DECADES

Here's the final remarkable twist. After the war, the Ghost Army's work was so sensitive, deception being a tactic the military wanted to keep in its playbook, that the entire operation was classified. For more than 40 years, these men couldn't tell anyone what they'd really done in the war. Their story stayed secret until the 1990s.

Finally, decades later, their extraordinary service was recognized. In 2022, the surviving members of the Ghost Army, by then very old men, were awarded the Congressional Gold Medal, one of the nation's highest honors, for their unique and daring contribution to victory.

WHY IT'S UNFORGETTABLE

The Ghost Army is proof that winning a war takes more than firepower, it takes cleverness, creativity, and nerve. A group of American artists and designers, armed with balloons and loudspeakers and their own imaginations, went to the front lines of the deadliest war in history and beat the enemy not with bullets, but with a brilliant, elaborate bluff.

They couldn't fire their guns or drive their tanks. But by making the enemy believe in an army that wasn't there, the men of the Ghost Army saved thousands of their fellow soldiers and helped win the war. It's one of the most ingenious, unlikely, and genuinely American stories of World War II, and for decades, almost no one knew it ever happened.

Not long ago, the idea of a laser weapon that shoots aircraft out of the sky belonged in science fiction. Then the US Army built one and used it. Now, America has taken the next big step: it's putting that laser weapon into full production, the first time in the entire history of the US military that a laser weapon has been ordered off the assembly line.

A HISTORIC FIRST

This week, the US Army awarded a contract worth roughly $465 million to build a fleet of laser weapons designed to destroy enemy drones. According to the manufacturer, it marks the first production contract for a directed-energy weapon, a laser, in US military history.

That's a genuine milestone. For decades, the military has been developing and testing laser weapons, working to move them from the laboratory to the battlefield. This contract means that phase is over. America isn't just experimenting with laser weapons anymore. It's building them in quantity and putting them in the hands of soldiers.

HOW IT WORKS

The weapon is called the Enduring High Energy Laser, and it's built to solve one of the biggest problems on the modern battlefield: cheap, swarming drones.

Instead of firing an expensive missile to knock down an incoming drone, this system fires a 30-kilowatt laser beam, an invisible bolt of concentrated energy that heats a drone until it fails and falls out of the sky. And here's the part that makes it a game-changer: because it's a laser, it never really runs out of ammunition in the traditional sense. As long as the system has electrical power, it can keep firing, essentially reloading itself through its own power supply.

Think about what that means against a swarm of drones. A laser can fire again, and again, and again, for a tiny fraction of the cost of a missile, basically just the cost of the electricity to power each shot. When the enemy is sending cheap drones by the dozen, that ability to keep firing affordably isn't just useful, it's essential.

BUILT FOR SOLDIERS, ANYWHERE

The Army is buying dozens of these laser systems, and one of their strengths is flexibility. The weapon isn't locked to a single vehicle, it can be mounted on different platforms, including standard military trucks, so it can move with soldiers wherever they go and protect them on the front lines.

The system builds directly on earlier laser prototypes that US soldiers are already using in the field, and on successful testing at White Sands Missile Range in New Mexico. In other words, this isn't an unproven concept, it's a tested capability now moving into full production, exactly as it should.

As one senior Army general put it, this "first-of-its-kind" laser program will let American forces "defeat unmanned systems and dominate from the outset," adding that "pairing human ingenuity with advanced technology is what ensures our Army will continue to outpace America's adversaries."

WHY IT MATTERS

Drones have transformed modern warfare. They're cheap, they're everywhere, and enemies can launch them in swarms to overwhelm defenses. Finding an affordable, reliable way to knock them down has become one of the most urgent challenges facing every military on earth.

America's answer, a laser that can burn drones out of the sky for pennies a shot, and keep doing it as long as it has power, is one of the most promising solutions anyone has come up with. And now it's leaving the test range and going into production.

For years, laser weapons were the technology of tomorrow, always a few years away. With this contract, tomorrow has arrived. American soldiers are about to be equipped with real, working laser weapons, and the country that built them has once again turned science fiction into battlefield reality.

Some of the most recognizable and feared aircraft in the American arsenal just touched down on the other side of the world. A task force of US Air Force B-52 Stratofortress bombers has landed in northern Australia, a powerful show of American airpower in the Pacific, and a sign that the United States and its close ally are strengthening their partnership for the challenges ahead.

THE BOMBERS ARRIVE

The aircraft, B-52H Stratofortresses from the 2nd Bomb Wing at Barksdale Air Force Base in Louisiana, landed this week at Royal Australian Air Force Base Tindal, in Australia's Northern Territory, about 200 miles from the city of Darwin.

The Air Force confirmed that a "B-52 Bomber Task Force is underway in Australia," saying the missions "bolster regional security across the region." For operational security reasons, the military kept the specific details of the mission under wraps, but the message of the deployment itself was unmistakable: American strategic bombers, capable of striking targets anywhere on earth, are now operating from a partner nation in a critical part of the world.

A LEGEND OF AMERICAN AIRPOWER

There are few aircraft on earth as iconic as the B-52. First flown in the 1950s, the massive eight-engine bomber has been a symbol of American strength for some 70 years, and it's still going strong, expected to keep flying for decades more. It can carry an enormous payload of weapons across intercontinental distances, and its very presence anywhere in the world sends a clear signal.

Deploying these bombers to Australia puts that reach and that firepower in position to help safeguard one of the most strategically important regions on the planet, alongside one of America's most trusted allies.

A DEEPENING ALLIANCE

The bombers' arrival is part of something bigger: a significant strengthening of the partnership between the United States and Australia.

The US has already funded major upgrades at Base Tindal specifically to host American bombers, including a new bomber ramp and hangar worth hundreds of millions of dollars. And American and Australian defense leaders have agreed to go further still, accelerating plans to base more US forces in Australia, work more closely together, run more joint exercises, and even jointly build and stockpile missiles and other weapons so both nations can draw on them.

There are also plans, under a partnership between the United States, the United Kingdom, and Australia, for American and British submarines to begin rotating through a base in Western Australia in the coming years. Piece by piece, the US and its allies are building a stronger, more connected military presence across the Pacific.

WHY IT MATTERS

The reason for all of this is no secret. Australia's defense minister pointed directly to what he called the largest conventional military buildup by any nation since World War II, taking place in China. In response, the United States and its allies are working to ensure they have the strength, the presence, and the readiness to keep the peace and deter any aggression in the region.

That's where aircraft like the B-52 come in. Strategic bombers are one of the clearest expressions of national power there is. They can project force across vast distances, and stationing them alongside a steadfast ally, within reach of a vital region, sends a message that words never could: that America and its partners are present, prepared, and standing together.

The B-52 has been reassuring America's friends and giving its adversaries pause for seven decades. Now, as the balance of power shifts in the Pacific, these old warhorses are doing it once again, on a runway in Australia, facing toward the horizon.

It was designed to carry soldiers into battle, not to destroy enemy tanks. For years before it ever saw combat, it was mocked, criticized, and called a failure. And then, in the deserts of Iraq in 1991, the humble M2 Bradley did something no one expected: it destroyed more Iraqi armored vehicles than the mighty M1 Abrams, America's own main battle tank. This is the surprising story of one of the most underestimated war machines America ever built.

A ROUGH START

The Bradley Fighting Vehicle had one of the most troubled developments of any American military vehicle. The Army spent something like 17 years wrestling the design through delay after delay, cancellation after cancellation, trying to build a vehicle that could keep pace with the fast new M1 Abrams tank while carrying a squad of infantry into the fight.

The result drew heavy criticism. Skeptics called it an over-budget compromise that did nothing well, too lightly armored to be a tank, too cramped to carry many troops, an awkward machine that couldn't decide what it was. By the time it entered service in 1981, the Bradley had become something of a punchline, a symbol, to its critics, of everything wrong with military procurement.

Then it went to war, and rewrote its own reputation.

WHAT IT WAS ACTUALLY BUILT TO DO

First, it helps to understand the Bradley's real job. It's not a tank. It's an infantry fighting vehicle, a fast, tracked machine designed to carry a small squad of soldiers into battle, protect them along the way, and then support them with firepower once they dismount.

To do that job, the Bradley was given real teeth: a rapid-firing 25mm chain gun capable of shredding lighter vehicles and enemy positions, and, crucially, TOW anti-tank guided missiles. Those missiles were the key. They meant that this "troop carrier" could, when it needed to, reach out and destroy an enemy tank from a distance. It was a capability the critics badly underestimated.

DESERT STORM: THE UNDERDOG DELIVERS

In 1991, during Operation Desert Storm, the Bradley finally got its chance to prove itself in a massive ground war against a large, tank-heavy Iraqi army. Around 2,200 Bradleys rolled into the fight alongside the Abrams tanks.

What happened stunned even the Army. Over the 100 hours of ground combat, the Bradley, the vehicle built to carry infantry, destroyed more Iraqi armored vehicles than the M1 Abrams tank did. Let that sink in. The troop carrier out-killed the tank. Using its TOW missiles and its chain gun, the Bradley knocked out enemy armor, including Iraqi T-72 tanks, in numbers that exceeded America's premier tank-killing machine.

And it did so while protecting its people remarkably well. Of the roughly 2,200 Bradleys in the war, only three were lost to enemy fire. The vehicle that critics said was too fragile turned out to be tough, fast, deadly, and dependable, exactly when it counted most.

BELOVED EVER SINCE

That performance transformed the Bradley's reputation forever. The mocked, troubled "failure" had become one of the most effective and respected combat vehicles in the world.

In the decades since, the Bradley has kept proving itself. It's served across multiple wars, been upgraded again and again, and protected countless American soldiers. More recently, it's fought in Ukraine, where Ukrainian crews have praised it lavishly for its firepower, its toughness, and its ability to keep them alive, so much so that even enemy forces who captured Bradleys reportedly studied them with admiration. More than 6,000 were built, and after 40-plus years, it remains the backbone of America's armored infantry.

WHY IT MATTERS

The story of the Bradley is a lesson in not judging too soon. Here was a machine dragged through a miserable, embarrassing development, ridiculed as a boondoggle, written off before it ever fired a shot in anger. And then it went to war and outperformed the very tank it was only supposed to support.

Sometimes the most underestimated tool turns out to be the most valuable one. The M2 Bradley wasn't supposed to be a tank-killer. It became one anyway, and in doing so, it earned the trust of generations of American soldiers who've ridden into battle behind its armor and come home because of it. Not bad for a vehicle everyone once loved to mock.

US forces have launched a new barrage of strikes against Iranian targets around the Strait of Hormuz, according to US Central Command, the latest development in an escalating exchange between the two countries.

WHAT'S HAPPENING

US Central Command, which oversees American military operations in the Middle East, said the strikes targeted Iranian forces in the area of the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow, strategically vital waterway at the mouth of the Persian Gulf through which a significant share of the world's oil passes.

The strikes are the most recent in a back-and-forth series of exchanges. In recent days, US forces struck Iranian targets, Iran responded by launching missiles and drones at bases hosting American troops in the region, and the US has now carried out further strikes. American officials have described their actions as responses to Iranian attempts to threaten commercial shipping and US forces in the area, including efforts to lay sea mines in the strait.

THE BROADER CONFLICT

This exchange is part of a wider conflict between the United States and Iran that has been ongoing for months. After a period of relative calm, direct fighting has flared up again around the Strait of Hormuz in recent days.

The stakes are significant. The Strait of Hormuz is one of the most important waterways in the world for global energy supplies, and both sides have focused military activity there. US forces recently cleared Iranian sea mines from international shipping lanes in the strait to keep commercial traffic moving.

The conflict has come at a real cost. According to the Pentagon's casualty figures, more than 750 US service members have been wounded and 18 have been killed since the fighting began earlier this year. Thousands of American troops remain deployed across the region, and some units have had their deployments extended.

WHERE THINGS STAND

The situation remains fluid and is developing rapidly. US officials have characterized the strikes as limited and precise, aimed at Iranian military forces rather than a broader campaign, but the rapid succession of strikes and counterstrikes reflects a tense and volatile moment.

As with any fast-moving military situation, details are still emerging and the picture may change. What is clear is that American and Iranian forces are engaged in an active and escalating exchange around one of the world's most critical waterways, and thousands of US troops are in the middle of it. We'll continue to follow the situation as more verified information becomes available.

Our thoughts are with the American service members deployed to the region and their families.

After an extraordinary stretch at sea, the sailors and Marines of the USS Abraham Lincoln are finally back on solid ground. The aircraft carrier steamed into the port of Laem Chabang, Thailand, on Wednesday morning, ending a remarkable 286 consecutive days at sea, and giving its exhausted crew the rest they've more than earned.

THE ARRIVAL

The Lincoln, carrying roughly 5,000 sailors and Marines, pulled into the Thai port after one of the longest continuous deployments in modern US Navy history, a stretch that included a long and demanding tour in the Middle East. The ship will remain in Thailand for about five days of rest and recuperation, a chance for the crew to finally step off the ship and recover.

Thailand is a fitting place to come ashore. It's the United States' only treaty ally in mainland Southeast Asia, a long-standing partner, and a welcoming port for American sailors after months at sea.

WHAT 286 DAYS ACTUALLY MEANS

It's hard for most people to grasp what a deployment of that length asks of a person. Aircraft carrier crews normally get a port visit roughly once a month, a chance to rest, resupply, and reconnect with the world. The sailors of the Lincoln went far, far longer than that.

Two hundred and eighty-six days is more than nine months, the vast majority of it spent in the same steel passageways, working long shifts, thousands of miles from home. No weekends off. No drive home at the end of a shift. No dinner with family, no walk outside, just the ship, the mission, and the ocean in every direction, day after day after day. It takes a rare kind of endurance to carry that, and to keep doing your job well the entire time. These sailors did.

WHO THEY ARE

It's easy to talk about a carrier in terms of steel and aircraft and firepower. But a warship is really its people, about 5,000 of them aboard the Lincoln, most of them young, many in their late teens and early twenties. They're somebody's son or daughter, somebody's husband or wife, somebody's mom or dad. They gave up the better part of a year of their lives, ordinary comforts, birthdays, holidays, milestones back home, because their country asked them to.

THE REST THEY'VE EARNED

For these sailors, reaching port means more than a logistical stop. It means a hot meal that didn't come from the ship's galley. A phone call home with a solid connection. A night's sleep somewhere quiet. The simple, enormous relief of standing on ground that doesn't move.

And soon, the bigger reward comes into view: the voyage home. Somewhere back in the United States, families are counting down the days, waiting for the moment every Navy family lives for, the carrier easing into its home port, the sailors lining the rails, and the reunions on the pier that make all those hard months mean something.

To the crew of the USS Abraham Lincoln: after 286 days at sea, you've earned every minute of this. Enjoy the ground beneath your feet. Rest up. And safe travels home. A grateful country is glad to have you back.

Some of the most dangerous work in the military happens quietly, underwater, out of sight. This week, US Navy divers and SEALs finished a mission that fits that description exactly: they cleared deadly Iranian sea mines from the Strait of Hormuz, one of the most important waterways on earth, and reopened the shipping lanes that had been shut down for months.

THE MISSION

The Strait of Hormuz is a narrow choke point at the mouth of the Persian Gulf, and it is one of the most vital stretches of water in the world. On a normal day, roughly a fifth of the entire world's oil supply passes through it. Choke that waterway, and you disrupt the global economy.

That's exactly what the sea mines threatened to do. Laid in the strait months earlier by Iran's Revolutionary Guard, these mines are deadly, hidden weapons designed to destroy or cripple any ship that comes near them. Their presence was one of the main reasons commercial shipping through the strait had been drastically reduced. The waterway was effectively being held hostage.

Clearing them fell to some of the most specialized people in the US military.

DANGEROUS WORK, DONE RIGHT

Removing sea mines is painstaking, nerve-wracking, and genuinely dangerous work. It means US Navy divers and SEALs going into the water, by hand, to locate and neutralize hidden explosives built to kill. There is very little margin for error. They did this work backed by coordinated air support from the Army, Air Force, Marines, and Navy, a true joint effort across the services.

And they succeeded. The top US commander in the region, Adm. Brad Cooper, announced that the mines had been cleared from the transit routes and praised what he called the "incredible work of the U.S. military."

"The circumstances were challenging and dangerous, to say the least, but we got the job done," Cooper said. "Bottom line, today international shipping lanes are open."

WHAT IT TOOK

The scale of the American presence behind this effort is significant. According to Cooper, there are around 50,000 US service members and more than 20 Navy ships operating across the region. Beyond clearing the mines, American forces provided coordinated protection to help guide nearly 1,500 commercial vessels safely through the strait, ships carrying close to 750 million barrels of crude oil bound for the world's markets.

In other words, American sailors and forces didn't just clear a path, they stood guard over it, escorting the civilian ships of global commerce through dangerous waters so the world's energy could keep flowing.

WHY IT MATTERS

It's easy to overlook a mission like this. There's no dramatic footage, no single moment of glory, just skilled, brave Americans doing quiet, deadly-dangerous work beneath the surface and getting it right. But the stakes could hardly be higher. A blocked Strait of Hormuz sends shockwaves through the entire global economy, driving up fuel prices and disrupting supply chains around the world.

American forces took on one of the most hazardous jobs there is, clearing hidden explosives by hand in open water, and they did it successfully, reopening a waterway the whole world depends on. It's a reminder of the reach and the skill of the US military, and of the men and women who take on the missions most people will never see. As their commander put it, the job was dangerous, but they got it done.

He wanted to be an American so badly that he enlisted in the United States Marine Corps the day after he received his green card. He wasn't yet a citizen. He didn't have to serve. But Rafael Peralta, born in Mexico City, loved his adopted country with everything he had, and four years later, in a house in Fallujah, he would give his life for it, and for the Marines beside him.

THE IMMIGRANT WHO COULDN'T WAIT TO SERVE

Rafael Peralta's story is, at its heart, an American one. Originally from Mexico City, he came to the United States and set his sights on becoming a Marine. He was so eager that the very day after he received his legal residency, his green card, in the year 2000, he walked in and enlisted. He would later become a proud US citizen, and he kept a copy of the Constitution and his boot camp graduation certificate on the wall of his San Diego home.

By November 2004, Sergeant Peralta was in Iraq, in the middle of the Second Battle of Fallujah, the fiercest, deadliest urban combat American troops had faced since the Vietnam War. It was a brutal, house-to-house fight to clear the city of entrenched insurgents.

A MARINE WHO PUT HIS BROTHERS FIRST

Even before his final act, Peralta showed the kind of Marine he was. After three exhausting days of clearing houses, room by dangerous room, Peralta didn't have to be on the mission that came next. But he volunteered. He asked to join an under-strength squad that needed men, and the night before, he volunteered to stand guard duty so his fellow Marines could get some rest. That was who he was. He put his brothers first.

On the morning of November 15, 2004, Peralta's squad was clearing houses again. At the seventh house of the day, they pushed inside and opened the door to a back room, and were instantly ambushed by insurgents firing automatic weapons at close range. In the chaos of that first burst, Sergeant Peralta was shot and mortally wounded, falling to the floor.

THE GRENADE

What happened next is why Marines still speak Rafael Peralta's name with reverence.

As the insurgents broke off and fled the building, one of them threw a fragmentation grenade back toward the Marines. It landed on the floor, near the gravely wounded Peralta, and just feet away from several of his fellow Marines who had no way to escape the blast in time.

And Rafael Peralta, lying there mortally wounded, did the last thing his body would ever do. According to his citation and the Marines who were in that room, he reached out, swept the grenade underneath his own body, and absorbed the explosion with himself, shielding the men beside him from the blast.

One of those Marines, Robert Reynolds, was just five feet away. "If he didn't sweep it underneath his body," Reynolds said, "I would be dead." It's believed Rafael Peralta saved as many as six of his fellow Marines with that final act. He gave his own life, in his last conscious moment, so that they could live.

THE FIGHT FOR HIS HONOR

For his extraordinary heroism, Sergeant Rafael Peralta was posthumously awarded the Navy Cross, the second-highest award for combat valor the nation can give. In 2017, the US Navy commissioned a guided-missile destroyer, the USS Rafael Peralta, in his honor, so that his name now sails the seas aboard an American warship.

But many believe he deserves more. The Marines who were in that room have spent nearly two decades insisting that Peralta earned the Medal of Honor, the nation's highest award. His award became one of the most debated cases in modern military history, and while officials wrestled with the details, the men whose lives he saved never wavered in their testimony about what he did. Peralta's own family long held out, believing he deserved the Medal of Honor, before finally accepting the Navy Cross and donating it to the ship that bears his name.

And the fight isn't over. As recently as this year, lawmakers introduced a renewed effort to finally award Rafael Peralta the Medal of Honor, so that his sacrifice might receive the nation's ultimate recognition. As one of them put it, the Marines who survived that room "have spent decades bearing witness to Sgt. Peralta's valor," and they want that testimony honored at last.

WHY HE'S REMEMBERED

Rafael Peralta's story carries a special power. He wasn't born an American. He chose to be one, and he was so eager to serve this country that he couldn't wait a single day to sign up. He didn't have to be in that house in Fallujah. He volunteered, again and again, to be where the danger was, so that others wouldn't have to be.

And in his final moment, dying, he found the strength to do one last thing for the Marines he loved: he pulled that grenade close and took the blast himself. There is no greater love, and no greater proof of devotion to one's brothers and one's country, than that.

Rafael Peralta became an American by choice, and a hero by sacrifice. Whatever medal hangs beside his name, the Marines who walked out of that house alive have never doubted what he was. He was one of the bravest of them all.

They were a crew of misfits, the men other pilots didn't want. Their airplane was a wreck, a bomber the Army had thrown away as too damaged to fly. And together, these castoffs and their salvaged plane would fly the single most decorated air mission in American history. This is the story of the "Eager Beavers" and their B-17 Flying Fortress, "Old 666."

THE CREW NOBODY WANTED

In the South Pacific in 1943, a pilot named Jay Zeamer had a problem: he couldn't get his own bomber. His crew had a reputation for being undisciplined troublemakers, the kind of men other commanders were happy to hand off. So Zeamer did something unusual. He gathered up these so-called misfits, castoffs and rejects, into a crew of his own.

Then he needed a plane. The only one he could get was a battered B-17E that had been discarded, deemed too shot-up and worn out to fly again, sitting in a boneyard. Its serial number ended in 666, so they named it "Old 666."

And then this crew of rejects did something remarkable: they rebuilt that junked bomber with their own hands, and they turned it into a monster.

A FLYING ARSENAL

The Eager Beavers, as the crew came to be called because there was no dangerous job they wouldn't take, weren't content to just make Old 666 airworthy. They up-armed it into the most heavily armed bomber in the Pacific.

A standard B-17 carried around 10 machine guns. The crew nearly doubled that, cramming in 19 guns. They swapped single guns for twin mounts and upgraded them to heavier .50-caliber weapons. Zeamer even mounted a fixed machine gun at his own pilot's station, so he could aim the entire bomber like a giant fighter plane and shoot straight ahead. It was an audacious, homemade fortress, and it was about to be tested like few aircraft ever have.

THE IMPOSSIBLE MISSION

On June 16, 1943, Old 666 was handed a mission so dangerous it bordered on suicidal: fly alone, with no fighter escort, some 600 miles over open ocean and deep into enemy territory, to photograph the coast of Bougainville Island ahead of a planned Allied invasion.

Here was the cruel catch. To get usable photographs, the bomber had to fly perfectly straight and level for a long stretch over the target, no dodging, no evasive maneuvers, for more than 20 minutes. It had to hold steady and make itself a sitting target, right over one of the most heavily defended enemy areas in the Pacific.

And the enemy was waiting. As Old 666 began its photo run, a swarm of Japanese Zero fighters, by some accounts as many as 17, rose to intercept the lone American bomber and tore into it.

STRAIGHT AND LEVEL

What Jay Zeamer did next defines the whole mission. He refused to turn away. With the photos not yet complete, he held Old 666 straight and level, directly through the enemy assault, so the cameras could finish their work. He would not sacrifice the mission, even as his aircraft was being shredded around him.

The fight was ferocious. Zeamer, firing his forward gun, shot down an attacking Zero. In the nose of the plane, the bombardier, Lieutenant Joe Sarnoski, fought back furiously. Then a cannon blast tore into him, mortally wounding him and blowing him from his position.

And here Sarnoski did something that has echoed through military history ever since. Dying, knowing he was dying, he crawled back to his gun. He got behind it, and he kept firing at the enemy, downing another attacker, until he died at his post. He gave the last moments of his life to protect his crew.

Zeamer, too, was being torn apart. Shrapnel ripped through his legs and arms. The instrument panel was destroyed. The oxygen system was knocked out, forcing a desperate dive so the crew could breathe. But Old 666 got its photos.

THE LONG WAY HOME

After about 40 minutes of relentless combat, the surviving Zeros finally broke off and turned for home. That left the Eager Beavers with a shattered airplane, a dead and dying crew, and 600 miles of ocean between them and safety.

Jay Zeamer was critically wounded, drifting in and out of consciousness. But he refused to give up the controls of his airplane. Fading and reviving, he helped fly that crippled bomber all the way back, more than 600 miles, while his surviving crewmen tended each other's wounds and kept Old 666 in the air.

They made it. Just over eight hours after they'd taken off, Old 666 landed, riddled with nearly 187 bullet holes and five cannon shell strikes. Six of the nine men aboard had been killed or wounded. Zeamer was so gravely hurt that medics nearly gave him up for dead. He would spend many months in hospitals recovering. But the precious photographs, the whole point of the mission, had made it home.

THE MOST DECORATED CREW IN HISTORY

The nation recognized what these men had done. Both Jay Zeamer and Joe Sarnoski were awarded the Medal of Honor, Sarnoski's posthumously, making Old 666 one of only two American bomber crews in all of World War II to have two Medal of Honor recipients. And every one of the other seven crewmen received the Distinguished Service Cross, the second-highest award for valor there is.

No other American air crew has ever been so highly decorated for a single mission. The misfits, the rejects nobody wanted, flying a bomber that had been thrown away, became the most decorated aircrew in American history.

WHY IT MATTERS

There's something perfect about this story. These weren't the polished, by-the-book airmen. They were the troublemakers and the castoffs, flying a plane that had been left for scrap. And when they were handed the mission no one else wanted, they didn't just complete it, they flew it into legend.

It's a reminder that heroism doesn't come only from the people who look the part. Sometimes it comes from the misfits, the underdogs, the ones written off, who, when everything is on the line, discover they have more courage than anyone imagined. Jay Zeamer held his bomber steady through a firestorm to get the job done. Joe Sarnoski crawled back to his gun to die fighting for his brothers. And a beat-up plane named Old 666 carried them all into history.
